questions.q: Which cells of the adrenal cortex secrete aldosterone?
options: Zona fasciculata cells
Chromaffin cells of the medulla
Zona glomerulosa cells
Zona reticularis cells
questions.explain: Aldosterone is the main mineralocorticoid, made in the outer cortical zone (glomerulosa).

open.q: Which cells of the adrenal cortex secrete aldosterone?

questions.q: What are the main renal effects of aldosterone?
options: It increases water excretion only
It increases sodium and water reabsorption and potassium excretion
It increases bicarbonate excretion only
It increases potassium reabsorption and sodium excretion
questions.explain: It acts on principal cells of the late distal tubule and cortical collecting duct, raising sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion.

open.q: What are the main renal effects of aldosterone?
accept: increases sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion

questions.q: Which are the two strongest stimuli for aldosterone secretion?
options: Angiotensin II and a high plasma potassium
ADH and a low plasma calcium level
ACTH and a low plasma potassium level
ANP and a high plasma sodium level
questions.explain: Low plasma sodium and ACTH are only weak stimuli. ANP inhibits aldosterone release.

open.q: Name the two strongest stimuli for aldosterone secretion.

questions.q: Which of these does NOT stimulate renin release?
options: Decreased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
Increased NaCl delivery to the macula densa
Reduced renal perfusion pressure
Sympathetic stimulation of the JG cells
questions.explain: Renin is released when perfusion pressure falls (afferent arteriole acts as a baroreceptor), when sympathetic nerves are active, or when less NaCl reaches the macula densa. More NaCl suppresses it.

questions.q: Which organ makes angiotensinogen?
options: The liver
The adrenal cortex
The lungs
The kidney
questions.explain: Renin cleaves liver-derived angiotensinogen to angiotensin I, and ACE, mostly in lung endothelium, converts it to angiotensin II.

questions.q: Which set lists actions of angiotensin II correctly?
options: Stimulates aldosterone and ANP release and reduces sodium reabsorption
Stimulates aldosterone, ADH and thirst, and increases proximal tubule NaCl reabsorption
Inhibits ADH and aldosterone and dilates all arterioles
Inhibits aldosterone, stimulates ADH and reduces thirst
questions.explain: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure and ECF volume. It also constricts arterioles.

open.q: Name three actions of angiotensin II.

questions.q: How does angiotensin II affect the efferent arteriole?
options: It constricts it, helping to maintain GFR when perfusion pressure is low
It has no effect on the efferent arteriole at all
It constricts only the afferent arteriole, not the efferent
It dilates it, which lowers glomerular pressure and GFR
questions.explain: Efferent constriction keeps glomerular pressure up. When ACE inhibitors remove this effect, GFR can drop, especially if renal perfusion is already reduced.

open.q: How does angiotensin II affect the efferent arteriole?

questions.q: Which kidney cells secrete erythropoietin?
options: Renal cortical peritubular interstitial cells
Macula densa
Collecting-duct principal cells
Podocytes
questions.explain: The producers are fibroblast-like interstitial cells in the cortex, not the JG cells, which make renin. Chronic kidney disease destroys them, so erythropoietin falls.

questions.q: What is the main stimulus for erythropoietin release?
options: Reduced oxygen delivery to the kidney
A raised red blood cell count in the blood
High arterial blood pressure in the kidney
A high plasma sodium concentration
questions.explain: Both a low arterial PO2 and a low haemoglobin concentration reduce oxygen delivery and raise erythropoietin output.

open.q: What is the main stimulus for erythropoietin release?

questions.q: What does erythropoietin do?
options: It speeds up red cell production from bone marrow stem cells
It breaks down old red cells in the spleen
It stimulates platelet production from marrow cells
It increases iron absorption directly from the gut
questions.explain: Falling erythropoietin explains the normocytic anaemia of chronic kidney disease.

questions.q: Where in the kidney is 25-hydroxyvitamin D converted to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D?
options: In the glomerulus, inside the podocytes
In the mitochondria of proximal tubule cells
In the loop of Henle, in the thin limbs
In the collecting duct, in the principal cells
questions.explain: 1-alpha-hydroxylation takes place in the proximal convoluted and straight tubules. Without it, as in kidney failure, vitamin D stays inactive.

open.q: Where in the kidney is 25-hydroxyvitamin D converted to active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D?

questions.q: Which of these is an action of active vitamin D (calcitriol)?
options: It lowers plasma calcium by increasing urinary loss only
It inhibits mineralisation of new osteoid
It decreases calcium absorption from the gut
It increases absorption of calcium and phosphate from the gut
questions.explain: Calcitriol also increases calcium resorption from bone and ensures normal mineralisation of new bone.

open.q: Name an action of active vitamin D (calcitriol).

questions.q: Where is ADH synthesised?
options: In the anterior pituitary, in the pars distalis
In the adrenal cortex, in the zona glomerulosa
In the hypothalamus (supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei)
In cells of the posterior pituitary gland
questions.explain: It travels down axons and is released from the posterior pituitary (neurohypophysis).

questions.q: Which receptor and second messenger mediate the action of ADH on the collecting duct?
options: V1 receptor, raising IP3 and constricting vessels
V2 receptor, raising cAMP and inserting aquaporin-2 channels
Aldosterone receptor, raising cGMP
Beta-2 receptor, lowering cAMP
questions.explain: Increased cAMP activates protein kinase A, which moves aquaporin-2 into the luminal membrane so water can leave the duct.

open.q: Which receptor and second messenger mediate the action of ADH on the collecting duct?

questions.q: Which is the strongest stimulus for ADH release?
options: A rise in blood volume
A fall in plasma osmolality
Drinking alcohol
A rise in plasma osmolality
questions.explain: Reduced blood volume and blood pressure, nausea and vomiting, nicotine and morphine also stimulate ADH.

open.q: Which is the strongest stimulus for ADH release?

questions.q: Which of these inhibits ADH secretion?
options: Nausea and vomiting
Morphine
Nicotine
Alcohol
questions.explain: Alcohol inhibits ADH, which is why drinking it produces a water diuresis.

open.q: Name a substance that inhibits ADH secretion.

questions.q: Which nerves carry baroreceptor information about falling blood volume to the nucleus tractus solitarius, leading to ADH release?
options: The facial and trigeminal nerves
The vagus and glossopharyngeal nerves
The hypogastric and splanchnic nerves
The pelvic and pudendal nerves
questions.explain: The signal relays from the nucleus tractus solitarius to the hypothalamic nuclei.

open.q: Which nerves carry baroreceptor information about falling blood volume to the nucleus tractus solitarius, leading to ADH release?

questions.q: What stimulates release of atrial natriuretic peptide?
options: Hypoxia of the kidney's cortical tissue
A fall in blood volume in the circulation
A raised plasma ADH level in the blood
Increased blood volume stretching the atria
questions.explain: Stretched atrial muscle cells secrete ANP.

open.q: What stimulates release of atrial natriuretic peptide?

questions.q: What are the effects of ANP?
options: It stimulates renin, aldosterone and ADH release
It inhibits renin, aldosterone and ADH, causing sodium loss and diuresis
It constricts the afferent arteriole to lower GFR
It increases sodium reabsorption in the collecting duct
questions.explain: ANP lowers ECF volume and blood pressure. It works against the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system.

open.q: What are the effects of ANP?

questions.q: A patient with bilateral renal artery stenosis develops hypertension. Which change in the juxtaglomerular apparatus initially drives activation of the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system?
options: Reduced afferent arteriolar perfusion pressure stimulates renin release
Increased renal perfusion pressure stimulates renin release
Increased macula densa NaCl delivery stimulates renin release
Raised plasma calcium directly stimulates renin release
questions.explain: Reduced pressure in the afferent arteriole is sensed by juxtaglomerular granular cells and promotes renin secretion, activating angiotensin II and aldosterone formation.

questions.q: A patient with heart failure is given an ACE inhibitor. Which effect contributes to the drug's reduction of afterload?
options: Reduced formation of angiotensin II causes systemic arteriolar vasodilation
Increased angiotensin II causes widespread vasoconstriction
Increased aldosterone causes sodium retention
Increased ADH causes water retention
questions.explain: ACE inhibition reduces angiotensin II formation, lowering systemic vascular resistance and afterload. It also reduces aldosterone secretion and sodium retention.

questions.q: A patient with advanced chronic kidney disease has normocytic normochromic anaemia. Which renal endocrine defect is the principal cause?
options: Reduced erythropoietin production by renal interstitial cells
Excessive renin secretion
Reduced aldosterone synthesis by zona glomerulosa
Increased renal calcitriol activation
questions.explain: Loss or dysfunction of renal peritubular interstitial erythropoietin-producing cells reduces stimulation of erythroid progenitors, causing a typically normocytic anaemia.

questions.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease develops hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism. Which renal defect contributes directly to this disturbance?
options: Reduced conversion of 25-hydroxyvitamin D to calcitriol by 1-alpha-hydroxylase
Increased conversion of calcitriol to 25-hydroxyvitamin D
Excessive calcitonin secretion by renal tubules
Increased intestinal activation of vitamin D
questions.explain: Diseased kidneys have reduced proximal tubular 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, lowering calcitriol production and intestinal calcium absorption. Hypocalcaemia and phosphate retention promote secondary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.q: A patient with central diabetes insipidus receives desmopressin. Which renal response is expected?
options: Increased aquaporin-2 insertion in collecting-duct principal cells and increased urine concentration
Reduced collecting-duct water permeability and increased dilute urine
Inhibition of sodium reabsorption in the proximal tubule
Increased potassium secretion caused by mineralocorticoid-receptor blockade
questions.explain: Desmopressin activates V2 receptors on collecting-duct principal cells, increasing cAMP and apical aquaporin-2 insertion. Water reabsorption rises and urine volume falls.

questions.q: Atrial natriuretic peptide promotes sodium excretion partly by which renal action?
options: Increasing glomerular filtration and reducing tubular sodium reabsorption
Increasing renin release from juxtaglomerular cells
Stimulating aldosterone secretion
Increasing collecting-duct aquaporin-2 insertion
questions.explain: ANP promotes natriuresis through haemodynamic and tubular effects, including increased filtration under appropriate conditions and reduced sodium reabsorption. It also suppresses renin and aldosterone.

questions.q: After several days of sustained aldosterone excess, sodium excretion may return towards intake despite continued hormone elevation. What is this phenomenon called?
options: Aldosterone escape
Pressure natriuresis failure
Atrial natriuretic peptide deficiency
Renal autoregulatory shutdown
questions.explain: Aldosterone escape limits progressive extracellular-fluid expansion. Increased arterial pressure and natriuretic mechanisms restore sodium balance, although potassium loss may persist.

questions.q: Renal tissue hypoxia increases erythropoietin gene expression mainly through stabilisation of which transcriptional regulator?
options: Hypoxia-inducible factor
Nuclear factor kappa B
Sterol regulatory element-binding protein
Signal transducer and activator of transcription 6
questions.explain: Under low oxygen conditions, prolyl hydroxylation of hypoxia-inducible factor is reduced. HIF-alpha escapes degradation, enters the nucleus and promotes erythropoietin transcription.

questions.q: In addition to its renal V2 effect, vasopressin can raise vascular smooth-muscle tone through which receptor?
options: V1 receptor
V2 receptor
Mineralocorticoid receptor
Nicotinic receptor
questions.explain: Vasopressin acts on V1a receptors on vascular smooth muscle, activating phospholipase C and increasing intracellular calcium to cause vasoconstriction.

questions.q: A fall in effective circulating volume increases sympathetic activity. Which adrenergic receptor on juxtaglomerular cells mediates the resulting increase in renin release?
options: Beta-1 receptor
Alpha-1 receptor
Beta-2 receptor
Alpha-2 receptor
questions.explain: Sympathetic stimulation of beta-1 receptors on juxtaglomerular granular cells increases renin secretion and activates the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system.
